subject: chemistry
title: Condensation polymers
key_idea: Condensation polymers form when monomers with two functional groups join and lose a small molecule each time. Polyesters link by ester bonds and polyamides by amide bonds. These links can be hydrolysed, so the polymers can biodegrade, unlike poly(alkenes).

blocks.text: In condensation polymerisation, monomers join and a small molecule, usually water or HCl, is lost at each link. This section covers the type of monomer needed.

items.meaning: A polymer made by joining monomers with the loss of a small molecule at each link.
The smallest section of the chain that repeats. Its bonds at each end go on to join the next unit.
A molecule with a –COOH group at each end, e.g. hexanedioic acid, HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH.

items: Each monomer has **two functional groups**, one at each end, so it can join to two others.
A **polyester** forms from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol (two –OH groups), or from a hydroxycarboxylic acid.
A **polyamide** forms from a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine (two –NH₂ groups), or from an amino acid.
A dicarboxylic acid can be replaced by its acyl chloride (a dioyl chloride). Then HCl is lost, not water.
Condensation monomers have two functional groups.
Acid + alcohol groups give polyesters; acid + amine groups give polyamides.
A small molecule (H₂O or HCl) is lost at every link.

blocks.text: Each polymer type is named after the link between its repeat units. This section covers how each forms and the common examples.

blocks.label: Making a polyester
where: The link –COO– is an ester link
One H₂O is lost for each ester link formed

blocks.label: Making a polyamide
where: The link –CONH– is an amide (peptide) link
Using a dioyl chloride instead of the acid loses HCl

items: A monomer with both groups, such as a hydroxycarboxylic acid HO–R–COOH or an aminocarboxylic acid H₂N–R–COOH, can join to itself.
Typical uses: Terylene for fibres in clothing and for bottles; nylon 6,6 for ropes, fabrics and gears; Kevlar for bulletproof vests and protective clothing.
Between chains of **polyesters**, there are permanent dipole–dipole attractions between the polar C=O and C–O bonds, and London forces.
Between chains of **polyamides**, there are strong hydrogen bonds between N–H and C=O groups, so the fibres are strong.
Kevlar's rigid benzene rings and regular hydrogen bonding between chains make it especially strong.
Polyesters have –COO– links; polyamides have –CONH– links.
Nylon 6,6, Terylene and Kevlar are the standard examples.
Hydrogen bonding between polyamide chains makes strong fibres.

blocks.text: You may be asked to work from monomers to a repeat unit, or from a section of polymer back to its monomers. This section gives the method.

items.text: Identify the two functional groups on each monomer, e.g. –COOH and –OH.
Take –OH from the acid and –H from the alcohol or amine (or Cl from an acyl chloride).
Form the new ester or amide link. Show open bonds at both ends of the repeat unit.

items: Nylon 6,6 repeat unit: –[NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO]–.
Terylene repeat unit: –[OCH₂CH₂OCO–C₆H₄–CO]–, with the benzene ring joined at positions 1 and 4.
For an amino acid H₂NCHRCOOH, the repeat unit is –[NHCHRCO]–.

items.text: Locate each ester (–COO–) or amide (–CONH–) link.
Split the link and add –OH to the C=O carbon (or Cl for an acyl chloride).
Add H to the O or N on the other side. The pieces are the dicarboxylic acid and the diol or diamine.

rows: Two functional groups, e.g. –COOH and –OH or –NH₂
Fewer atoms than the monomers combined

diagram.alt: Sort each monomer or pair of monomers by the type of polymerisation.
diagram.prompt: Which type of polymerisation does each monomer, or pair of monomers, undergo?

items: Repeat unit: join the monomers, lose the small molecule, and show open bonds at both ends.
Monomers: break each ester or amide link and restore –OH and –H.
C=C monomers give addition polymers; two functional groups give condensation polymers.

blocks.text: Polyesters and polyamides contain polar links that water can attack. This section covers hydrolysis, and how it compares with poly(alkenes).

items: **Acid hydrolysis**: heating with aqueous acid breaks the ester or amide links. A polyester gives a dicarboxylic acid and a diol; a polyamide gives a dicarboxylic acid and the diamine as its ammonium salt.
**Base hydrolysis**: heating with aqueous alkali gives the diol (from a polyester) or the diamine (from a polyamide), and the dicarboxylic acid as its sodium salt.
Hydrolysis is the reverse of the condensation that made the polymer.
The C=O carbon in an ester or amide link is δ+, so it can be attacked by water, H⁺ or OH⁻. Polyesters and polyamides are therefore biodegradable.
**Poly(alkenes)** have only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds. They are chemically inert and are difficult to biodegrade.
Some polymers can also be broken down by the action of **light** (photodegradable polymers).

rows: Uses land; non-biodegradable polymers remain for years
Releases energy that can generate electricity
Produces CO₂ and can release toxic gases, e.g. HCl from PVC

items: Polyesters and polyamides are hydrolysed by acid or alkali because their links are polar.
Poly(alkenes) are inert and non-biodegradable.
Disposal methods each have advantages and disadvantages.

checks.q: Draw the repeat unit of the polyamide formed from hexanedioic acid and hexane-1,6-diamine, and state the small molecule lost.
checks.a: –[NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO]– with open bonds at both ends. Water is lost at each link.

checks.q: The section –OCH₂CH₂OCO–C₆H₄–CO– is part of a polymer chain. Name the type of polymer and give the two monomers.
checks.a: It is a polyester (condensation polymer). The monomers are ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid.

checks.q: Explain why polyesters can be hydrolysed but poly(ethene) cannot.
checks.a: Polyesters have ester links with a polar C=O group, so the δ+ carbon is attacked by water, H⁺ or OH⁻. Poly(ethene) has only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds, so it is chemically inert and not attacked.

blocks.text: This part covers the products of hydrolysis of each polymer and the prediction skills for both types of polymer.

items: Polyester + aqueous acid: dicarboxylic acid + diol. Polyester + aqueous alkali: dicarboxylate salt + diol.
Polyamide + aqueous acid: dicarboxylic acid + diammonium salt. Polyamide + aqueous alkali: dicarboxylate salt + diamine.
For an addition polymer, the repeat unit is the monomer with its C=C opened: propene gives –[CH₂CH(CH₃)]–.
Given a section of chain, decide the type: a carbon-only chain is addition; ester or amide links mean condensation.

blocks.text: This part covers the ways a polymer can be broken down and the prediction skills.

items: Polyesters and polyamides are biodegradable through **acidic and alkaline hydrolysis**.
Poly(alkenes) are inert, so they are difficult to biodegrade.
Some polymers are degraded by light, which breaks bonds in the chain.
Predict the type of polymerisation from the monomers: C=C gives addition; two functional groups give condensation.
Deduce the type from a polymer section in the same way: look for the ester or amide link.
